title: Why Colombia’s ELN Guerrillas Have Never Made Peace
gist: Using a newly public last interview of ex-ELN commander Ricardo Lara Parada, the author argues the ELN has always killed moderates and dissenters, which is why it never made peace. At about 6,000 fighters, flush with cocaine and gold revenue, it will likely outlast the offensive promised by new president De La Espriella.

insights.claim: The ELN murdered ex-commander Ricardo Lara Parada in 1985, sent by former comrades, because he was building a peaceful political alternative in the group's own territory after accepting amnesty.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Illustrates the pattern that moderation inside the group gets punished.
insights.locator: But in 1985, Lara was gunned down

insights.claim: Throughout its history the ELN has used violence to crush dissent and moderation, a key reason it has never made peace.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Negotiation prospects should be discounted given the group's internal dynamics.
insights.quote: throughout its history, the ELN has used violence to crush dissent and moderation

insights.claim: The ELN executed critics of founder Fabio Vasquez, including co-founder Victor Medina Moron in 1968, and in 1974 executed three urban commanders as traitors, later conceding they were innocent; Lara said the mentality was that of the Inquisition.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Evidence of a command culture that rejects reformers.
insights.quote: Our mentality was the same mentality as the Inquisition.

insights.claim: When an ELN dissident front broke away, negotiated separately and disarmed, the leadership read it as Bogota fragmenting its chain of command, so the show of moderation hardened rather than softened its posture.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Split-and-negotiate tactics can backfire with this group.
insights.locator: Critically, when an ELN dissident front

insights.claim: Every government from Betancur onward opened talks with the ELN that ultimately fell apart, including Uribe's exploratory talks after the 1999 Cali church kidnapping of 190, Santos's process, and Duque's, which the ELN ended in 2019 with a car bomb killing 22 police cadets.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Base rate: no Colombian administration has secured a deal.

insights.claim: Under Gustavo Petro, talks reached their furthest point in 2024 with an agreed transition model, but the ELN refused to stop ransom kidnapping, assaulted a military base and attacked a FARC dissident group in Catatumbo, killing scores and displacing 50,000, so Petro broke off talks.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Even the most favorable conditions failed, lowering odds for future talks.

insights.claim: The ELN has about 6,000 members present in an estimated 19 Colombian departments and at least seven Venezuelan states, using drones and car bombs, and is a key factor in Colombia's deteriorating security.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Security risk for Colombian infrastructure, notably oil pipelines and rural operations.

insights.claim: After most of the FARC demobilized the ELN expanded into FARC areas and, despite earlier vows, now taxes or participates in cocaine and illicit gold trafficking, both at record highs, funding weapons and rivaling the Clan del Golfo in strength.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Illicit-economy windfalls remove the incentive to settle.
insights.locator: After most of the FARC demobilized

insights.claim: The ELN was rebuilt after Operation Anori by Manuel Perez in Arauca just as oil was discovered, with pipeline extortion funding recovery; it has bombed pipelines since 1964.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Energy infrastructure has been the ELN's financing and target for decades.

insights.claim: President Abelardo De La Espriella, inaugurated August 7, promises to end all peace talks and launch a major military offensive against the ELN, likely with renewed military cooperation with Washington.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Expect higher violence and security risk in ELN zones near term.

insights.claim: The ELN's decentralized structure, with fronts holding their own finances and a command that coordinates rather than dictates, makes decapitation less effective than against the FARC, so the group will probably survive and a settlement may be further than ever.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: Do not price a quick security resolution into Colombia risk.
insights.locator: Even so, if history is any guide

insights.claim: The US capture of Nicolas Maduro could jeopardize the Venezuelan safe haven where many ELN fighters are based and whose authorities treated it as a paramilitary ally.
insights.speaker: LUIS DANIEL GONZÁLEZ
insights.so_what: A Venezuelan policy shift is a second pressure point on the ELN.
insights.locator: In the wake of the U.S. capture of Nicolás Maduro
